desc:
On a social site with n accounts, follows[i][j] = 1 means account i follows account j. Following does not have to be returned: follows[i][j] and follows[j][i] can differ. The diagonal entries follows[i][i] carry no information.

Two accounts are in the same circle if you can get from one to the other by a chain of accounts where each neighbouring pair is linked by a follow in either direction. Return the number of circles.

follows = [[0,1,0],
           [0,0,0],
           [0,0,0]]

result = 2     (accounts 0 and 1 form a circle; account 2 is alone)
constraints: follows is an n x n matrix with entries 0 or 1
follows[i][j] and follows[j][i] may differ; follows[i][i] may be 0 or 1
hints: Ignore directions: a follow from i to j connects the two accounts just as much as a follow from j to i.
This is the number-of-provinces problem, except that the matrix does not have to be symmetric. Treat follows[i][j] = 1 as an undirected link.
Start with n groups and union i with j whenever follows[i][j] == 1 (check every ordered pair, or both [i][j] and [j][i] for each pair). Every successful merge reduces the number of circles by one.
editorial: Start with every account in its own set, circles = n. Scan the whole matrix; for each cell (i, j) with i != j and value 1, find the roots of i and j and merge them if they differ, decreasing the counter. Because every ordered pair is visited, a one-sided follow is enough to link two accounts, and the diagonal is skipped.

The answer is the number of sets left. Time is O(n² · α(n)) since the matrix has n² cells. A common mistake is to only read the upper triangle (j > i), which silently drops follows that appear only below the diagonal.
